story_title: The Moon and the Slow Clock

script:
[[CHAPTER Welcome]]

Welcome to Fernwick Nights. Tonight's story is The Moon and the Slow Clock, told by Aldous Reed, who was stationmaster at Fernwick Halt and still winds its clock. Get comfortable, pull your coat a little closer, and let the time pass at its own pace.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Slow Clock]]

Step inside and take the bench by the stove. The last train is not for an hour, and the kettle is already humming. Now, you will have looked up at the clock over the door, and you will have thought that it was wrong. It is, a little. And here is the question I am asked more than any other. Why does the clock at Fernwick Halt run two minutes slow on the nights of the full moon? Tonight the moon is only a thin silver curl, hardly there at all, but I will tell you anyway, because it is a good tale and the evening is long.

[pause]

I should explain who I am. For thirty-four years I stood on this platform in a navy coat with brass buttons, and I blew a whistle at trains that had already seen me. Now I am retired, and my only duty is the clock. Each night at the same hour I climb the little ladder, open the glass face, and wind the key until it gives a soft, round click. The waiting room has six wooden benches, a black stove with a kettle on it, and a timetable so old that two of the towns on it have changed their names.

[pause]

The room smells of tea, coal smoke, toast and oiled floorboards, with the damp wool of coats that have been hung up to dry. The stove ticks as it warms. The benches have been polished by a hundred years of travelers, and each one has a faint dip in the middle, like a shallow bowl. On the wall there is a brass lamp with a green glass shade, which throws a circle of soft light onto the timetable and leaves the corners of the room in friendly shadow.

[pause]

[[CHAPTER Where the Tale Comes From]]

The tale is much older than the station. It comes from ancient Greece, and it was told for a very long time before anyone wrote it down. Poets sang it, and then grandmothers told it, and by the time the Romans got hold of it, it had traveled across the whole sea. It is about the Moon, who the Greeks called Selene, and a young shepherd called Endymion, and a hill called Latmos, on the coast of what is now Turkey.

[pause]

The hill is real. It rises beside a lake, among gray boulders the size of houses, and the people who live near it will still show you a cave and tell you that it is the one. I have never been there. A traveling clockmender once showed me a postcard of it, brown at the edges, and I kept it in the drawer of my desk for years. The rocks are pale and the grass is sparse, and the whole place looks as if it has been left in the sun to dry.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Shepherd on the Hill]]

So. Imagine a warm evening, a very long time ago. Endymion has led his sheep up the slope, counted them twice, and settled them in a hollow where the thyme grows thick. The air smells of dust, wild herbs and warm stone. He carries a wooden crook and a flat loaf of bread wrapped in cloth, still smelling of woodsmoke. He sits down on a flat rock, eats half the loaf slowly, and gives the rest to the nearest sheep, who accepts it without comment.

[pause]

There are twenty sheep, and each of them has a name, though only Endymion remembers them all. There is Barley, who is round and slow, and Thistle, who is gray and suspicious, and a lamb called Pocket, who follows him everywhere because she believes, with great confidence, that he is her mother. Their bells make a thin, scattered chime across the hill, like a handful of small coins being dropped one at a time into a jar.

[pause]

He is a quiet young man, and he has a habit that is considered strange in his village. He likes to watch the sky. Not for the weather, as the other shepherds do, but simply to look. He lies back in the grass with his hands behind his head and watches the stars come out one by one, as if someone were lighting lamps along a very long street.

[pause]

Above him, the Moon is rising. She is rising early tonight, a pale round shape in the blue, and she has noticed the shepherd. In the old stories she rides across the heavens every night in a silver cart, pulled by two white horses, and she has seen a great many things from up there: sleeping cities, ships at anchor, foxes in the snow. But she has never seen anyone look back at her quite so kindly.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Silver Cart]]

She slows the horses a little. It is very hard to explain how a moon slows down, but the old tellers all agree that she did. The light on the hillside turns from white to the soft yellow of milk, and the shadows of the boulders grow long and gentle. The sheep lift their heads, one after another, and look at the sky with mild surprise.

[pause]

The cart is made of silver light, with two high wheels as thin as the rims of cups. The horses are white as new snow, and they puff small clouds of mist that drift across the sky and become the thin clouds you sometimes see around the moon. They are very patient animals. They have pulled that cart through every night since the world began, and they know a good moment to stop when they see one.

[pause]

Endymion has fallen asleep. It happened gradually, the way it does, one thought at a time, and now he lies in the grass with his crook across his chest and his mouth a little open. His loaf is gone. The thyme is warm beneath his shoulders, and the crickets have started up in the dry grass. The Moon looks down at him for a long time, and the horses stand quite still.

[pause]

Then she does something that no moon had done before. She steps down from her cart, which is not at all easy, and she comes to the hill herself. Her feet make no sound on the grass. The light follows her like a dress. She sits beside him on the flat rock, folds her hands in her lap, and does nothing at all. She only watches him sleep, and the sheep, who are very discreet, look the other way.

[long pause]

Every night after that, she comes back. When the sky has been dark for an hour and the village below has gone to bed, the Moon leaves her cart on the ridge and visits the cave on the hill. She lays one pale hand of light on his forehead. She smooths the blanket. She counts the sheep. And before the first gray of morning, she climbs into her cart again, with a small, contented sigh, and carries on across the sky.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Two Minutes]]

That is the whole of the tale, as I like to tell it. There are other endings, but they are for other evenings. In mine, the shepherd sleeps on, warm and untroubled, and the Moon keeps coming back, and neither of them ever seems to mind.

[pause]

Now, you may be wondering about the clock. I will tell you. I have kept this station for a very long time, and I have noticed that on the nights of the full moon, a great white light comes in through the east window and falls across the stove, the benches and the old timetable. It lies there, quiet and enormous. And one night, years ago, I thought that if the Moon is going to take the trouble to look in on all of us, the least I can do is give her a little extra time.

[pause]

So on those nights, I turn the minute hand back by two minutes. The trains do not mind. The timetable is a rough thing, anyway. And the Moon, I like to think, has a moment longer to sit by the window, and warm her hands at our stove, and look at the sleepers on the benches before she must go.

[pause]

I will admit that not everyone approves. Last winter, a man with a briefcase and a very firm manner looked up at the clock, then at his own wristwatch, and informed me that my station was running slow. I told him that it was running slow on purpose, and that the Moon was visiting. He looked at me for a long moment. Then he bought a cup of tea, and sat down on the nearest bench, and said that in that case he supposed he was in no hurry either.

[pause]

[long pause]

The kettle is still humming, and the steam smells faintly of tea. A moth has found the lamp and is going round it in slow, tired circles. Out on the platform the gravel is cool and pale, and the single line of rail shines faintly in the starlight. You are welcome to put your feet up on the next bench, and I will not tell the stationmaster, who is, as it happens, me.

[long pause]

[[SECOND]]

[[CHAPTER Once More, Slowly]]

Why does the clock run two minutes slow on the nights of the full moon? Because of a shepherd, and the Moon.

[pause]

Endymion lies on a warm hill. He looks at the stars. He falls asleep in the thyme.

[long pause]

The Moon slows her horses. She steps down from her silver cart. She sits beside him, and she watches.

[pause]

Every night she comes. She smooths the blanket. She counts the sheep.

[long pause]

So Aldous Reed turns the clock back two minutes, to give the Moon a little more time at the window.

[long pause]

And that is the story of the Moon and the slow clock. The stove is warm, and the bench is yours for as long as you like. The last train can wait. Good night.
